applications.h: Why transmission lines are aluminium, not copper
applications.d: Copper conducts better, but aluminium is far lighter and much cheaper, and for overhead lines strung between pylons weight decides the engineering. Household wiring uses copper because the runs are short and conductivity matters more than mass. Silver is the best conductor of all and is used only where cost is irrelevant, such as in specialised contacts.

applications.h: The thermistor in your appliances
applications.d: A thermistor is a semiconductor whose resistance falls sharply as temperature rises. That behaviour, the opposite of a metal, makes it an excellent temperature sensor: measure the resistance and you know the temperature. Thermistors sit inside refrigerators, air conditioners, ovens and battery packs, and they exist precisely because of the negative temperature coefficient that defines a semiconductor.

applications.h: Why solar panels are silicon
applications.d: A photon with enough energy can lift an electron across silicon’s 1.1 eV band gap, creating a free electron and a hole. A p-n junction then separates them and drives a current through an external circuit. A conductor cannot do this — its bands overlap, so there is no gap to cross and no way to convert light into a directed current. The band gap is not a defect; it is the entire mechanism.

applications.h: Doping is what makes modern electronics possible
applications.d: Adding roughly one impurity atom per million silicon atoms can raise conductivity enormously and decide whether electrons or holes carry the current. That controllability is why a semiconductor can switch and amplify while a conductor can only carry. Every transistor, integrated circuit, LED and microprocessor rests on it.

numericals.q: Calculate the resistance of a copper wire of length 2 m and cross-sectional area 1 × 10⁻⁶ m², given resistivity 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.
numericals.answer: 0.034 Ω. The very low resistivity of a conductor is why such a wire offers almost no resistance.

numericals.q: A silicon sample has a band gap of 1.1 eV. Express this energy in joules. (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
steps: Energy in joules = energy in eV × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹.
numericals.answer: 1.76 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Any photon carrying at least this much energy can free an electron in silicon.

boardQuestions.q: Distinguish between conductors, semiconductors and insulators on the basis of energy bands and resistivity.
boardQuestions.a: In a conductor the valence band and the conduction band overlap, or the conduction band is only partly filled, so electrons need virtually no additional energy to move and current flows freely. Resistivity is very low, of the order of 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ ohm metre, and examples are silver, copper and aluminium. In a semiconductor there is a small forbidden energy gap between the two bands, about 1.1 eV in silicon and 0.7 eV in germanium. At absolute zero a pure semiconductor behaves as an insulator, but at room temperature thermal energy lifts some electrons across the gap. Resistivity lies between roughly 10⁻⁵ and 10⁶ ohm metre. In an insulator the forbidden gap is large, generally above 3 eV, so under ordinary conditions almost no electrons can cross it and virtually no current flows; resistivity exceeds about 10⁸ ohm metre, and examples are rubber and glass.

boardQuestions.q: Why does the resistance of a conductor increase with temperature while that of a semiconductor decreases?
boardQuestions.a: In a conductor the number of free electrons is already very large and does not change appreciably with temperature. Heating simply makes the lattice atoms vibrate more vigorously, so the drifting electrons collide with them more frequently, their motion is impeded, and the resistance rises. A conductor therefore has a positive temperature coefficient of resistance. In a semiconductor the number of charge carriers is small at room temperature and depends strongly on temperature. Heating supplies energy that lifts additional electrons across the small forbidden gap into the conduction band, creating both free electrons and holes. This large increase in the number of carriers far outweighs the increased collisions, so the net resistance falls. A semiconductor therefore has a negative temperature coefficient of resistance.

boardQuestions.q: What is doping? Distinguish between n-type and p-type semiconductors.
boardQuestions.a: Doping is the deliberate addition of a very small, controlled quantity of a suitable impurity to a pure semiconductor in order to increase its conductivity greatly and to determine which kind of charge carrier predominates. The resulting material is called an extrinsic semiconductor. An n-type semiconductor is produced by adding a pentavalent impurity such as phosphorus, arsenic or antimony, which has five valence electrons. Four form covalent bonds with the surrounding silicon atoms and the fifth is left loosely bound and easily freed, so electrons become the majority carriers and holes the minority carriers. A p-type semiconductor is produced by adding a trivalent impurity such as boron, aluminium or gallium, which has only three valence electrons. One bond is left incomplete, creating a hole, so holes become the majority carriers and electrons the minority carriers. In both cases the material remains electrically neutral overall, because no net charge has been added.

boardQuestions.q: What is a hole? Explain how it contributes to conduction.
boardQuestions.a: When an electron gains enough energy to leave its position in a covalent bond and move into the conduction band, it leaves behind a vacancy in the valence band. This vacancy is called a hole, and because the absence of a negative charge leaves a local excess of positive charge, a hole behaves as a positive charge carrier. Conduction occurs when a neighbouring valence electron moves into the hole, filling it but creating a new hole at its own former position. Repeated many times, this makes the hole appear to travel through the material in the direction opposite to the movement of the electrons. A semiconductor therefore conducts by both electrons and holes, whereas a conductor conducts by free electrons alone.

assertionReason.assertion: The resistance of a semiconductor decreases as temperature increases.
assertionReason.reason: Heating frees additional electrons across the small forbidden energy gap.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. The increase in charge carriers outweighs the increased lattice collisions.

assertionReason.assertion: A pure semiconductor behaves as an insulator at absolute zero.
assertionReason.reason: At absolute zero no electron has enough thermal energy to cross the forbidden gap.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and correctly linked. The conduction band is empty, so no current can flow.

assertionReason.assertion: An n-type semiconductor carries a net negative charge.
assertionReason.reason: Electrons are the majority carriers in an n-type semiconductor.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is false — the material stays electrically NEUTRAL, since each donor atom contributes a positive nucleus along with its extra electron. The reason is true and is precisely the fact students misread as implying net charge.

assertionReason.assertion: Silicon is preferred over germanium in most devices.
assertionReason.reason: Silicon has a larger band gap and so is less affected by temperature.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and correctly linked. Silicon’s 1.1 eV gap against germanium’s 0.7 eV gives better high-temperature stability, and silicon is also cheaper and more abundant.

glossary.def: A material with abundant free electrons and very low resistivity (10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ Ω m). Copper, aluminium, silver.
A material whose conductivity lies between a conductor and an insulator, controllable by doping. Silicon, germanium.
A material with a forbidden gap above about 3 eV, so almost no current flows. Rubber, glass.
The energy band containing the outermost bound electrons of the atoms.
The energy band in which electrons are free to move and carry current.
The energy separation between valence and conduction bands. ~1.1 eV in silicon, ~0.7 eV in germanium.
The vacancy left when an electron leaves a covalent bond. Behaves as a positive charge carrier.
Adding a controlled trace impurity to raise conductivity and set the majority carrier.
Doped with a PENTAVALENT impurity (phosphorus, arsenic). ELECTRONS are the majority carriers.
Doped with a TRIVALENT impurity (boron, gallium). HOLES are the majority carriers.
A pure, undoped semiconductor with equal numbers of electrons and holes.
Resistance FALLS as temperature rises — the defining behaviour of a semiconductor.

revision: CONDUCTOR: bands OVERLAP, resistivity 10⁻⁸-10⁻⁶ Ω m, resistance RISES with temperature.
SEMICONDUCTOR: small gap (~1.1 eV Si, 0.7 eV Ge), resistance FALLS with temperature.
INSULATOR: gap > 3 eV, effectively no conduction.
The temperature reversal is THE most-examined contrast in this topic.
Semiconductors conduct by ELECTRONS **and** HOLES. Conductors use electrons only.
PENTAVALENT doping (P, As) → n-type, electrons majority. TRIVALENT (B, Ga) → p-type, holes majority.
Doping does NOT charge the material — it stays electrically neutral overall.
Silicon beats germanium: larger gap, better heat stability, cheaper, forms a usable oxide.

explainers.term: Speed at an instant
paras: Speed is the distance travelled by an object in unit time: speed = distance ÷ time. It is a scalar quantity, meaning it has magnitude but no direction, and its SI unit is metre per second (m/s). Kilometre per hour is also common, and the conversion is 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s.
When people say 'the car was doing 60', they mean instantaneous speed — the speed at that particular moment, which is what a speedometer shows. It can change from second to second.

explainers.term: Average speed over a journey
paras: Average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken. It is a single number that summarises a whole journey, however irregular that journey was.

The definition is the important bit: total distance over total time. It is NOT the average of the individual speeds. A car that covers half a journey at 40 km/h and the other half at 60 km/h does not average 50 km/h — it averages 48 km/h, because it spends more time at the slower speed. This trap appears in exams constantly.

sections.h: Uniform and non-uniform motion
paras: An object is in uniform motion when it covers equal distances in equal intervals of time, however small those intervals. In that special case, the instantaneous speed and the average speed are the same number.

In non-uniform motion the object covers unequal distances in equal intervals — which describes almost all real motion, such as a bus in traffic. Here the instantaneous speed keeps changing, and the average speed is the only single figure that describes the whole journey.

sections.h: Speed versus velocity, and average velocity
paras: Speed is a scalar and uses distance, which is the total path length covered. Velocity is a vector and uses displacement, which is the shortest straight-line distance from start to finish, with direction.

So average speed = total distance ÷ total time, but average velocity = total displacement ÷ total time. For an object that returns to its starting point, the displacement is zero, so the average velocity is zero — even though the average speed is clearly not. A runner completing one lap of a track is the standard example.
Average velocity can also be found as (initial velocity + final velocity) ÷ 2, but only when the acceleration is uniform. Applying that shortcut to non-uniform motion is a common error.

sections.h: The two-part journey formula
paras: For a journey covered in two equal distances at speeds a and b, the average speed is 2ab ÷ (a + b) — the harmonic mean, not the arithmetic mean. For 40 and 60 that gives (2 × 40 × 60) ÷ 100 = 48 km/h.

But if the two speeds are maintained for equal times rather than equal distances, the average genuinely is (a + b) ÷ 2 = 50 km/h. Read the question carefully to see whether it is equal distances or equal times — the two give different answers, and examiners know it.

examples.t: A car covering 120 km in 3 hours
examples.d: Average speed = 120 ÷ 3 = 40 km/h, regardless of how much it sped up or slowed down along the way.

examples.t: A runner completing one full lap of a 400 m track in 50 s
examples.d: Average speed = 400 ÷ 50 = 8 m/s. Average velocity = 0, because the displacement is zero — she finished where she started.

examples.t: Half a trip at 40 km/h, half at 60 km/h
examples.d: Average speed = 2(40)(60) ÷ 100 = 48 km/h, not 50, because more time is spent on the slower half.

examples.t: A speedometer reading 55 km/h
examples.d: Instantaneous speed — the speed at that exact moment, not the average for the journey.

mistakes: Averaging the two speeds directly when the distances are equal. Use 2ab ÷ (a + b) instead.
Using displacement in an average-speed calculation. Average speed uses total distance travelled.
Saying average velocity and average speed are always equal in magnitude. They are equal only when the motion is in a straight line without reversing.
Applying average velocity = (u + v) ÷ 2 to non-uniform acceleration. It holds only for uniform acceleration.
Forgetting the unit conversion: 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s, not 18/5.

quiz.q: A body covers 100 m in 20 s and the next 100 m in 30 s. Its average speed is:
quiz.why: Total distance 200 m, total time 50 s, so 200 ÷ 50 = 4 m/s. Averaging 5 and 3.33 would wrongly give 4.17.

quiz.q: A runner completes exactly one lap of a circular track. Her average velocity is:
quiz.why: She ends where she began, so her displacement is zero and average velocity = displacement ÷ time = 0.

quiz.q: Which quantity is a vector?
quiz.why: Velocity has both magnitude and direction. Speed, distance and time are scalars.

quiz.q: 72 km/h expressed in m/s is:
quiz.why: Multiply by 5/18: 72 × 5 ÷ 18 = 20 m/s.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between speed and average speed?
extraFaqs.a: Speed usually means the instantaneous speed — how fast an object is moving at one particular moment, which is what a speedometer shows. Average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken for the whole journey, and it smooths out all the variations along the way.

extraFaqs.q: Can average speed be zero?
extraFaqs.a: Only if the object never moves at all. Average speed uses total distance, which can never be negative and is zero only if no distance was covered. Average velocity, by contrast, is zero whenever an object returns to its starting point.

extraFaqs.q: Why is the average of 40 km/h and 60 km/h not 50 km/h?
extraFaqs.a: Because over equal distances the object spends more time travelling at the slower speed, so the slower speed carries more weight. The correct formula for equal distances is 2ab ÷ (a + b), which gives 48 km/h. If the two speeds were held for equal times instead, the answer would genuinely be 50 km/h.

extraFaqs.q: Can an object have constant speed but changing velocity?
extraFaqs.a: Yes. An object moving in a circle at a steady rate has constant speed, but its direction changes continuously, so its velocity is changing. That is why circular motion at constant speed still involves acceleration.

applications.h: What your speedometer does and does not tell you
applications.d: A speedometer shows instantaneous speed — how fast you are moving at this exact moment. It says nothing about the journey as a whole. A trip computer showing "average 42 km/h" is doing something different: dividing total distance by total time, including every traffic light and jam. This is why a drive that touched 80 km/h can still average 35 — the stops count in the time but add nothing to the distance.

applications.h: Average speed cameras on highways
applications.d: Older cameras measured instantaneous speed at one point, so drivers braked for the camera and accelerated after. Average-speed enforcement reads a number plate at two points a known distance apart and divides distance by time. Because it measures the whole stretch, braking for one camera achieves nothing. It is a direct, practical use of the definition — and it is why the two quantities must never be confused.

applications.h: Why athletics uses average speed
applications.d: A 100 m sprinter finishing in 10 s has an average speed of 10 m/s, but she did not run at 10 m/s throughout — she started from rest, accelerated for roughly the first 40 m, and peaked well above 11 m/s. The average conceals the variation, which is exactly what an average is for and exactly why coaches use split times to see the detail underneath it.

applications.h: Estimating travel time realistically
applications.d: Route planners quote an average speed far below the road’s speed limit because they build in junctions, traffic and stops. Multiplying distance by the limit gives a time no journey achieves. Using a realistic average speed instead is the everyday application of total distance over total time, and it is why 200 km on an Indian highway rarely takes the two hours a 100 km/h limit suggests.

numericals.q: A car covers the first 100 km at 50 km/h and the next 100 km at 100 km/h. Find its average speed for the whole journey.
steps: Time for the first stretch = 100 ÷ 50 = 2 h.
Time for the second stretch = 100 ÷ 100 = 1 h.
Total distance = 100 + 100 = 200 km. Total time = 2 + 1 = 3 h.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 200 ÷ 3.
numericals.answer: 66.67 km/h — NOT 75 km/h. Averaging the two speeds is wrong because more time is spent on the slower stretch. The shortcut 2ab/(a+b) = 2(50)(100)/150 gives the same 66.67.

numericals.q: A boy runs 400 m around a circular track in 100 s and returns to his starting point. Find his average speed and average velocity.
steps: Average speed = total DISTANCE ÷ total time = 400 ÷ 100 = 4 m/s.
He finishes exactly where he began, so his DISPLACEMENT is zero.
numericals.answer: Average speed 4 m/s; average velocity 0 m/s. This is the standard illustration that speed uses distance while velocity uses displacement.

numericals.q: A train travels at 60 km/h for 30 minutes, then at 40 km/h for the next 45 minutes. Find its average speed.
steps: Convert times to hours: 30 min = 0.5 h, 45 min = 0.75 h.
Total distance = 60 km. Total time = 0.5 + 0.75 = 1.25 h.
numericals.answer: 48 km/h.

boardQuestions.q: Define speed and average speed. How do they differ?
boardQuestions.a: Speed is the distance travelled by an object per unit time, and in ordinary use it means instantaneous speed — the speed at a particular moment, which is what a speedometer displays. Average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken for the whole journey. The difference is one of scope: instantaneous speed describes a single instant and can change continuously, while average speed summarises an entire journey in one number and conceals all the variation within it. They are equal only when the motion is uniform, that is when the object covers equal distances in equal intervals of time.

boardQuestions.q: Distinguish between distance and displacement, and hence between speed and velocity.
boardQuestions.a: Distance is the total length of the path actually covered by a moving object, regardless of direction. It is a scalar quantity, is always positive, and can never decrease during a journey. Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance between the initial and final positions, together with the direction. It is a vector quantity, can be positive, negative or zero, and its magnitude is always less than or equal to the distance. Speed is distance divided by time, so it is a scalar and is always positive. Velocity is displacement divided by time, so it is a vector with both magnitude and direction. The clearest illustration is an athlete completing one full lap of a circular track: the distance is the full circumference so her average speed is non-zero, but her displacement is zero because she ends where she started, so her average velocity is zero.

boardQuestions.q: A car travels the first half of a distance at 40 km/h and the second half at 60 km/h. Find its average speed and explain why it is not 50 km/h.
boardQuestions.a: Let the total distance be 2d. Time for the first half is d divided by 40, and for the second half d divided by 60. The total time is therefore d/40 + d/60, which is (3d + 2d)/120 = 5d/120 = d/24. Average speed is total distance over total time, that is 2d divided by d/24, which gives 48 km/h. It is not 50 km/h because average speed weights by TIME, not by distance, and the car spends longer on the slower half of the journey. The general formula for two equal distances is 2ab/(a+b), which here gives 2 × 40 × 60 ÷ 100 = 48 km/h. Note that if the two speeds were maintained for equal TIMES rather than equal distances, the answer genuinely would be 50 km/h.

boardQuestions.q: When are the average speed and the magnitude of average velocity equal?
boardQuestions.a: They are equal only when the distance travelled equals the magnitude of the displacement, which happens when the object moves along a straight line in one fixed direction without reversing. In that case the path length and the straight-line separation between start and finish are the same. If the object changes direction, doubles back, or moves along a curved path, the distance exceeds the magnitude of the displacement, so the average speed becomes greater than the magnitude of the average velocity.

boardQuestions.q: Define uniform and non-uniform motion with an example of each.
boardQuestions.a: An object is in uniform motion when it covers equal distances in equal intervals of time, however small those intervals are taken to be; its speed does not change, so instantaneous and average speed are identical. An example is a car moving steadily at 60 km/h on a straight empty highway. An object is in non-uniform motion when it covers unequal distances in equal intervals of time, so its speed keeps changing. An example is a bus travelling through city traffic, repeatedly slowing at junctions and accelerating away. Almost all real motion is non-uniform, which is why average speed is such a useful summary.

assertionReason.assertion: The average speed of a body can be zero only if it never moves.
assertionReason.reason: Average speed is total distance divided by total time, and distance is never negative.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and correctly linked. Distance can only accumulate, so the only way the total is zero is if no motion occurred. Average velocity, by contrast, is zero whenever the body returns to its start.

assertionReason.assertion: A car travelling half a journey at 40 km/h and half at 60 km/h averages 50 km/h.
assertionReason.reason: The average of two numbers is their sum divided by two.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is false — over equal DISTANCES the answer is 48 km/h, because more time is spent at the lower speed. The reason is a true statement of arithmetic that simply does not apply here.

assertionReason.assertion: An object moving in a circle at a steady rate has zero acceleration.
assertionReason.reason: Its speed does not change.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is false: the direction of the velocity changes continuously, so the object is accelerating. The reason is true but describes speed, not velocity.

assertionReason.assertion: The magnitude of displacement can never exceed the distance travelled.
assertionReason.reason: Displacement is the shortest path between the initial and final positions.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. The shortest route between two points cannot be longer than any actual path taken between them.

Equal DISTANCES at a and b → 2ab/(a+b). Equal TIMES at a and b → (a+b)/2. Read which one is given.
40 and 60 over equal distances = 48 km/h, not 50. This is the most-set trap in the chapter.

explainers.term: Speed — how fast
paras: Speed tells you how much distance an object covers in unit time: speed = distance ÷ time. Its SI unit is metre per second (m/s), and it is a scalar, so it has size but no direction.
Speed answers the question 'how fast is it going right now?' A number on its own is enough — 20 m/s is a complete statement of speed.

explainers.term: Acceleration — how quickly the velocity changes
paras: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: a = (v − u) ÷ t, where u is the initial velocity and v the final velocity. Its SI unit is metre per second squared (m/s²), and it is a vector, so direction matters.

Acceleration answers a different question: 'how quickly is the motion changing?' An object can have a huge speed and zero acceleration — a train cruising steadily at 100 km/h — or zero speed and a large acceleration, like a ball at the exact top of its flight, momentarily still but still accelerating downward at 9.8 m/s².

sections.h: The three equations of motion
paras: These apply only to uniformly accelerated motion in a straight line. Almost every numerical in the chapter uses one of them.
bullets: v = u + at — relates velocity and time.
s = ut + ½at² — relates distance and time.
v² = u² + 2as — relates velocity and distance, with no time term. Use this one when time is not given and not asked for.
Here u is initial velocity, v final velocity, a acceleration, t time and s distance travelled.
For a body falling freely, replace a with g = 9.8 m/s² (often taken as 10 m/s² for quick working). For a body thrown upward, g is negative because it opposes the motion.

sections.h: Positive, negative and zero acceleration
paras: Acceleration is positive when velocity increases in the direction of motion — the object speeds up. It is negative when velocity decreases; this is called retardation or deceleration, and braking is the everyday case.

Acceleration is zero when velocity does not change at all, which means the object is at rest or moving with uniform velocity in a straight line. Zero acceleration does not mean zero speed, and that distinction is worth marks.

sections.h: Reading motion graphs
paras: On a distance-time graph, the slope gives the speed. A straight line means uniform speed; a curve means the speed is changing; a horizontal line means the object is at rest.

On a velocity-time graph, the slope gives the acceleration and the area under the graph gives the distance travelled. A horizontal line means uniform velocity and therefore zero acceleration; a straight sloping line means uniform acceleration. Being asked to find distance from the area under a velocity-time graph is a standard exam question.

examples.t: A car speeding up from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 4 s
examples.d: a = (30 − 10) ÷ 4 = 5 m/s². Its speed changed; the acceleration describes how quickly.

examples.t: A train cruising at a steady 100 km/h
examples.d: High speed, but zero acceleration — the velocity is not changing.

examples.t: A ball at the highest point of a throw
examples.d: Speed is zero for an instant, but acceleration is 9.8 m/s² downward. Speed and acceleration are genuinely independent.

examples.t: A car braking from 20 m/s to rest in 5 s
examples.d: a = (0 − 20) ÷ 5 = −4 m/s². The negative sign means retardation.

mistakes: Thinking zero speed means zero acceleration. A ball at the top of its flight disproves it.
Writing the unit of acceleration as m/s. It is m/s².
Using the equations of motion when the acceleration is not uniform. They only apply to uniform acceleration.
Forgetting that g is negative for a body thrown upward and positive for a body falling.
Confusing the slope and the area on a velocity-time graph: slope gives acceleration, area gives distance.

quiz.q: The SI unit of acceleration is:
quiz.why: Acceleration is the change in velocity (m/s) per unit time (s), giving m/s².

quiz.q: A body starts from rest and reaches 20 m/s in 5 s. Its acceleration is:
Which equation does NOT contain time?
quiz.why: v² = u² + 2as relates velocity to distance directly, which is why it is used when time is neither given nor asked for.

quiz.q: On a velocity-time graph, the area under the curve represents:
quiz.why: The slope gives acceleration; the area under the graph gives the distance travelled.

extraFaqs.q: Can an object have zero speed but non-zero acceleration?
extraFaqs.a: Yes. A ball thrown straight up is momentarily at rest at the highest point of its flight, so its speed is zero, but gravity is still acting on it and its acceleration is 9.8 m/s² downward. This is the standard example used to show that speed and acceleration are independent.

extraFaqs.q: What is negative acceleration called?
extraFaqs.a: Retardation, or deceleration. It occurs when the velocity decreases with time, such as when a vehicle brakes. The acceleration acts in the direction opposite to the motion.

extraFaqs.q: Can an object moving at constant speed be accelerating?
extraFaqs.a: Yes, if its direction is changing. An object moving in a circle at a steady rate has constant speed but continuously changing velocity, so it is accelerating. Acceleration responds to any change in velocity, including a change of direction alone.

extraFaqs.q: When do the equations of motion not apply?
extraFaqs.a: They apply only to motion with uniform acceleration along a straight line. If the acceleration is changing, or the path is curved, these three equations give wrong answers and calculus-based methods are needed instead.

applications.h: Why 0-60 figures describe acceleration, not speed
applications.d: A car advertised as "0 to 100 km/h in 7 seconds" is being sold on its acceleration, not its top speed. Two cars with the same maximum speed can feel utterly different because one reaches it far quicker. Acceleration is what you physically feel pressing you into the seat; steady speed, however high, feels like nothing at all, which is why a smooth aircraft at 900 km/h feels still.

applications.h: Free fall and why everything falls together
applications.d: Near the Earth’s surface every freely falling body accelerates at about 9.8 m/s² regardless of its mass, because gravity pulls harder on a heavier object but that object also resists acceleration more, and the two effects cancel exactly. A feather falls slower only because of air resistance; in a vacuum a feather and a hammer land together, as demonstrated on the Moon during Apollo 15.

applications.h: Stopping distance and road safety
applications.d: Braking supplies a retardation, and from v² = u² + 2as the stopping distance depends on the SQUARE of the initial speed. Doubling your speed roughly quadruples the distance needed to stop. This single relationship is the reason speed limits fall so sharply near schools, and it is a far more persuasive argument than any slogan.

applications.h: Circular motion: changing velocity at constant speed
applications.d: A stone whirled on a string at a steady rate has constant speed but continuously changing direction, so its velocity is changing and it is therefore accelerating. The acceleration points towards the centre and is supplied by the tension in the string. Cut the string and the stone flies off along the tangent — direct evidence that a force was needed simply to keep it turning.

numericals.q: A body starting from rest attains a velocity of 30 m/s in 6 s. Find its acceleration and the distance covered.
numericals.answer: Acceleration 5 m/s², distance 90 m.

numericals.q: A car moving at 20 m/s is brought to rest over 50 m. Find its retardation using v² = u² + 2as.
numericals.answer: Retardation of 4 m/s². Note this equation is the one to use when time is neither given nor asked for.

numericals.q: A stone is dropped from a height of 45 m. Find the time to reach the ground and its striking velocity. Take g = 10 m/s².
numericals.answer: It takes 3 s and strikes the ground at 30 m/s.

numericals.q: A bus accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 25 m/s in 5 s. Find the acceleration and the distance travelled.
numericals.answer: Acceleration 3 m/s²; distance 87.5 m. Check with v² = u² + 2as: 625 = 100 + 2(3)(87.5) = 100 + 525 = 625. Consistent.

boardQuestions.q: Define speed and acceleration. State their SI units and whether each is a scalar or a vector.
boardQuestions.a: Speed is the distance travelled by a body per unit time. Its SI unit is the metre per second (m/s) and it is a scalar quantity, having magnitude but no direction. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity of a body, given by the change in velocity divided by the time taken, a = (v − u)/t. Its SI unit is the metre per second squared (m/s²) and it is a vector quantity, having both magnitude and direction. The essential distinction is that speed tells you how fast a body is moving, whereas acceleration tells you how quickly that motion is changing.

boardQuestions.q: Write the three equations of motion and state the condition under which they are valid.
boardQuestions.a: The three equations are v = u + at, which relates velocity and time; s = ut + ½at², which relates distance and time; and v² = u² + 2as, which relates velocity and distance without involving time. Here u is the initial velocity, v the final velocity, a the acceleration, t the time taken and s the distance travelled. They are valid only for motion in a straight line with UNIFORM acceleration, that is when the acceleration does not change during the interval considered. If the acceleration varies, or the path is curved, these equations give incorrect results and calculus-based methods are required instead.

boardQuestions.q: Can a body have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration? Explain with an example.
boardQuestions.a: Yes. Velocity and acceleration are independent quantities, and a body can have one without the other. The standard example is a ball thrown vertically upward. At the highest point of its flight the ball is momentarily at rest, so its velocity is zero, but gravity continues to act on it throughout, so its acceleration is 9.8 m/s² directed downward. It is precisely because the acceleration is non-zero at that instant that the ball does not remain suspended but immediately begins to fall.

boardQuestions.q: Draw and describe what the slope and area of a velocity-time graph represent.
boardQuestions.a: On a velocity-time graph, velocity is plotted on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. The SLOPE of the graph represents the acceleration of the body, because slope is change in velocity divided by change in time, which is the definition of acceleration. A horizontal line therefore means zero acceleration and uniform velocity, while a straight sloping line means uniform acceleration. The AREA enclosed between the graph and the time axis represents the distance travelled, since velocity multiplied by time gives distance. For uniformly accelerated motion the area is a trapezium, and computing it gives the same result as the equation s = ut + ½at².

boardQuestions.q: A train starting from rest accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² for 10 s. Find its final velocity and the distance covered.
boardQuestions.a: Here the initial velocity u is 0 since the train starts from rest, the acceleration a is 2 m/s² and the time t is 10 s. Using the first equation of motion, v = u + at gives v = 0 + 2 × 10 = 20 m/s, so the final velocity is 20 m/s. Using the second equation, s = ut + ½at² gives s = 0 × 10 + ½ × 2 × 10² = ½ × 2 × 100 = 100 m, so the distance covered is 100 m. This can be checked with the third equation: v² = u² + 2as gives 400 = 0 + 2 × 2 × 100 = 400, which is consistent.

assertionReason.assertion: A body can have zero speed and non-zero acceleration.
assertionReason.reason: At the highest point of its flight a body thrown upward is momentarily at rest while gravity still acts.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and the reason is the standard example proving the assertion. Speed and acceleration are independent quantities.

assertionReason.assertion: Uniform circular motion is accelerated motion.
assertionReason.reason: The direction of the velocity changes continuously even though the speed is constant.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and correctly linked. Acceleration responds to any change in velocity, and direction is part of velocity.

assertionReason.assertion: The equations of motion apply to all kinds of motion.
assertionReason.reason: They relate the quantities u, v, a, t and s.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is false — they hold only for straight-line motion with UNIFORM acceleration. The reason is a true but incomplete statement that does not rescue it.

assertionReason.assertion: Doubling the speed of a car roughly quadruples its stopping distance.
assertionReason.reason: From v² = u² + 2as, the stopping distance depends on the square of the initial speed.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. This is the physics behind lower speed limits near schools.

galvanometer-and-ammeter.ncertRef: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 11 — Electricity; conversion using a shunt in Class 12 Physics, Chapter 4 — Moving Charges and Magnetism.

explainers.term: Galvanometer — a detector of tiny currents
paras: A galvanometer is an instrument that detects and measures very small electric currents. Its most distinctive feature is the scale: the zero sits at the centre, and the pointer can swing either side of it. That is what lets a galvanometer show the direction of the current as well as its presence.

It works on the magnetic effect of current: a coil carrying current in a magnetic field experiences a torque, and the pointer deflects by an amount proportional to that current. Because it is designed for sensitivity, a galvanometer has a fairly high resistance and can be damaged by any substantial current.

explainers.term: Ammeter — a measurer of ordinary currents
paras: An ammeter measures electric current in amperes, over the range found in ordinary circuits. Its zero sits at the left-hand end of the scale, not the centre, because it is normally used where the current direction is already known.

The defining electrical property of an ammeter is its very low resistance. It is always connected in series with the component whose current is being measured, and if it had appreciable resistance it would reduce the very current it is trying to measure. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance.

sections.h: Turning a galvanometer into an ammeter
paras: An ammeter is, in fact, a galvanometer that has been modified. Connect a very small resistance — called a shunt — in PARALLEL with the galvanometer coil, and most of the current bypasses the sensitive coil and flows through the shunt instead.

This does two things at once: it protects the delicate galvanometer from large currents, and it brings the combination's overall resistance down to the near-zero value an ammeter needs. The shunt value is given by S = I_g G ÷ (I − I_g), where G is the galvanometer resistance, I_g the current for full-scale deflection and I the maximum current to be measured.

sections.h: And into a voltmeter — note the reversal
paras: A galvanometer becomes a voltmeter by connecting a HIGH resistance in SERIES with it. This is the exact opposite of the ammeter conversion, and swapping the two is the most common error in the topic.

The logic follows from how each instrument is used. An ammeter goes in series with the circuit, so it must have almost no resistance or it would change the current. A voltmeter goes in parallel across a component, so it must have very high resistance or it would draw current away and change the very voltage it is measuring. An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

sections.h: The comparison in one table
paras: These are the points examiners ask for by name.
bullets: Purpose — a galvanometer detects and measures very small currents and shows their direction; an ammeter measures current in amperes.
Zero position — galvanometer at the centre of the scale; ammeter at the left end.
Resistance — a galvanometer has relatively high resistance; an ammeter has very low resistance.
Direction — a galvanometer indicates the direction of current by which way the pointer deflects; an ordinary ammeter does not.
Connection — both are connected in series in the circuit, but only the ammeter is safe for ordinary currents.
Relationship — an ammeter is a galvanometer with a low-resistance shunt connected in parallel.

examples.t: Checking whether a circuit carries any current at all
examples.d: Use a galvanometer. It responds to currents far too small to move an ammeter needle.

examples.t: Measuring the 2 A drawn by a bulb
examples.d: Use an ammeter, connected in series with the bulb.

examples.t: A pointer deflecting to the left instead of the right
examples.d: A galvanometer showing that the current is flowing in the opposite direction.

examples.t: Adding a shunt of a fraction of an ohm across a galvanometer
examples.d: Converting it into an ammeter — the shunt carries most of the current and drops the overall resistance.

mistakes: Saying a shunt is connected in series. The shunt is in PARALLEL with the galvanometer; a series resistance makes a voltmeter instead.
Connecting an ammeter in parallel with a component. It must always be in series, and connecting it in parallel can short the component and damage the meter.
Claiming an ideal ammeter has infinite resistance. It has zero resistance; the voltmeter is the one with infinite resistance.
Forgetting that a galvanometer's zero is at the centre of the scale.
Assuming a galvanometer can measure large currents directly. It cannot, and will be damaged by them.

quiz.why: A low resistance shunt in parallel carries most of the current, protecting the coil and lowering the overall resistance as an ammeter requires.

quiz.q: An ammeter is always connected:
quiz.why: Current must pass through the ammeter for it to be measured, so it goes in series.

quiz.q: The zero of a galvanometer scale is usually located:
quiz.why: A centre zero lets the pointer deflect either way, showing the direction of the current as well as its magnitude.

options: The same resistance as the circuit
quiz.why: A voltmeter is connected in parallel, so infinite resistance ensures it draws no current and does not alter the voltage it measures.

extraFaqs.q: What is the main difference between a galvanometer and an ammeter?
extraFaqs.a: A galvanometer detects and measures very small currents and shows their direction, with the zero at the centre of its scale and a relatively high resistance. An ammeter measures ordinary currents in amperes, has its zero at the left end and a very low resistance. An ammeter is essentially a galvanometer fitted with a low-resistance shunt in parallel.

extraFaqs.q: Why must an ammeter have very low resistance?
extraFaqs.a: Because it is connected in series with the circuit. Any appreciable resistance would add to the circuit's total resistance and reduce the current, meaning the meter would alter the very quantity it is measuring. An ideal ammeter therefore has zero resistance.

extraFaqs.q: What is a shunt?
extraFaqs.a: A shunt is a very small resistance connected in parallel with a galvanometer to convert it into an ammeter. It provides an alternative path for most of the current, protecting the sensitive coil and bringing the overall resistance down. Its value is S = I_g G ÷ (I − I_g).

extraFaqs.q: Can a galvanometer be used as a voltmeter?
extraFaqs.a: Yes. Connecting a high resistance in series with a galvanometer converts it into a voltmeter. Note the contrast with the ammeter conversion, which uses a low resistance in parallel — the series-versus-parallel distinction is the point examiners test.

applications.h: Checking a circuit for any current at all
applications.d: A galvanometer detects currents far too small to move an ammeter needle, which is why it is the instrument of choice for null-point experiments such as the Wheatstone bridge and the metre bridge. There the aim is not to measure a value but to find the setting at which the deflection becomes exactly zero, and only a very sensitive centre-zero instrument can show that reliably.

applications.h: Why a wrongly connected ammeter destroys itself
applications.d: An ammeter has almost no resistance and must be connected in series. Connect it in parallel across a component and it short-circuits that component: an enormous current flows through the meter, and it is damaged or destroyed. A voltmeter, with very high resistance, fails the opposite way — placed in series it blocks the circuit so almost no current flows. Series for the ammeter, parallel for the voltmeter, and the reason is the resistance in each case.

applications.h: Reading the direction of a current
applications.d: Because a galvanometer’s zero sits at the centre of its scale, the pointer can swing either way, showing not only that current is flowing but which way. This matters when demonstrating electromagnetic induction: moving a magnet into a coil deflects the pointer one way and withdrawing it deflects the pointer the other, which is how Lenz’s law is shown experimentally.

applications.h: One movement, three instruments
applications.d: The same moving-coil galvanometer becomes an ammeter with a low resistance shunt in parallel, or a voltmeter with a high resistance in series, or an ohmmeter with an added cell. Understanding this makes the whole topic one idea rather than three, and it explains why a multimeter can switch between functions using a single movement.

numericals.q: A galvanometer of resistance 50 Ω gives full-scale deflection for 2 mA. What shunt is needed to convert it into an ammeter reading up to 1 A?
numericals.answer: S ≈ 0.1002 Ω, about 0.1 Ω. The shunt is very small, which is what drops the combination’s overall resistance to near zero as an ammeter requires.

numericals.q: The same galvanometer (G = 50 Ω, Ig = 2 mA) is to be converted into a voltmeter reading up to 10 V. Find the series resistance.
steps: For a voltmeter, R = (V ÷ Ig) − G.
numericals.answer: 4950 Ω in SERIES. Contrast this with the previous answer: a huge series resistance for a voltmeter, a tiny parallel one for an ammeter.

boardQuestions.q: Distinguish between a galvanometer and an ammeter.
boardQuestions.a: A galvanometer is an instrument used to detect and measure very small electric currents. Its zero is placed at the centre of the scale so the pointer can deflect either side, indicating the direction of the current as well as its presence, and it has a comparatively high resistance, which means a large current would damage it. An ammeter measures current in amperes over the range found in ordinary circuits. Its zero is at the left-hand end of the scale, it has a very low resistance, and an ideal ammeter would have zero resistance. Both are connected in series in a circuit. The relationship between them is that an ammeter is simply a galvanometer fitted with a low resistance, called a shunt, connected in parallel with its coil.

boardQuestions.q: Explain how a galvanometer is converted into (a) an ammeter and (b) a voltmeter.
boardQuestions.a: To convert a galvanometer into an ammeter, a very small resistance called a shunt is connected in PARALLEL with the galvanometer coil. Most of the current then bypasses the sensitive coil and flows through the shunt, which protects the galvanometer and simultaneously reduces the overall resistance of the combination to nearly zero, as an ammeter requires since it is connected in series. The shunt value is given by S = Ig G ÷ (I − Ig), where G is the galvanometer resistance, Ig the current for full-scale deflection and I the maximum current to be measured. To convert a galvanometer into a voltmeter, a high resistance is connected in SERIES with it. This limits the current drawn to a safe value and raises the overall resistance to a large value, as a voltmeter requires since it is connected in parallel across a component and must not draw appreciable current. The series resistance is R = (V ÷ Ig) − G. Noting that the two conversions are opposite in both the size of the resistance and its mode of connection is the key to the topic.

boardQuestions.q: Why is an ammeter connected in series and a voltmeter in parallel?
boardQuestions.a: An ammeter measures the current flowing through a component, and current can only be measured if it actually passes through the meter, which requires a series connection. For this not to disturb the circuit, the ammeter must have a very low resistance, since any appreciable resistance added in series would reduce the very current it is measuring; an ideal ammeter has zero resistance. A voltmeter measures the potential difference across a component, so it must be connected across it, that is in parallel. For this not to disturb the circuit, the voltmeter must have a very high resistance, since a low-resistance path in parallel would draw current away and reduce the potential difference it is measuring; an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

boardQuestions.q: What is a shunt? State two functions it performs.
boardQuestions.a: A shunt is a resistance of very small value connected in parallel with a galvanometer in order to convert it into an ammeter. It performs two functions. First, it protects the galvanometer: because it offers a much easier path, the greater part of the current passes through the shunt and only a small safe fraction flows through the delicate coil. Second, it lowers the effective resistance of the combination to a very small value, which is essential because the instrument is to be connected in series and must not alter the current in the circuit. Its value is calculated from S = Ig G ÷ (I − Ig).

assertionReason.assertion: An ammeter must have a very low resistance.
assertionReason.reason: It is connected in series and should not alter the current being measured.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Any appreciable series resistance would reduce the current the meter is trying to report.

assertionReason.assertion: A shunt is connected in series with a galvanometer to convert it into an ammeter.
assertionReason.reason: The shunt protects the galvanometer from large currents.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is false — the shunt goes in PARALLEL. The reason is true (it does protect the coil), which is exactly why this pairing traps students who remember the purpose but not the connection.

assertionReason.assertion: A galvanometer has its zero at the centre of the scale.
assertionReason.reason: It is designed to indicate the direction of the current as well as its magnitude.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and correctly linked. A centre zero lets the pointer deflect either way.

assertionReason.assertion: An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.
assertionReason.reason: It is connected in parallel and must draw no current from the circuit.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Drawing current would change the potential difference being measured.

solution-vs-suspension.ncertRef: NCERT Class 9 Science, Chapter 2 — Is Matter Around Us Pure?

explainers.term: Solution — a true, homogeneous mixture
paras: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances, meaning its composition is exactly the same throughout. The dissolved substance is the solute and the one doing the dissolving is the solvent; in salt water, salt is the solute and water the solvent.

The solute particles are extremely small — less than 1 nanometre across — so they are invisible even under a microscope, they pass straight through filter paper, they never settle on standing, and they do not scatter a beam of light. A solution is therefore transparent and stable.

explainers.term: Suspension — a heterogeneous mixture that settles
paras: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture in which solid particles are dispersed through a liquid without dissolving. The particles are large, greater than about 100 nanometres, and are big enough to be seen with the naked eye or a simple microscope.

Because the particles are so large, a suspension behaves in the opposite way to a solution at every point: it is unstable and settles out when left undisturbed, the particles are held back by filter paper, and it scatters light strongly. Muddy water left in a glass overnight shows all of this.

sections.h: The third type: colloids
paras: Between the two sits the colloid, and leaving it out costs marks. A colloid has particle sizes between roughly 1 and 1000 nanometres — larger than in a solution but smaller than in a suspension.

A colloid appears homogeneous to the eye but is actually heterogeneous. Its particles are too small to settle out and too small to be stopped by ordinary filter paper, yet large enough to scatter light. Milk, fog, smoke, ink and jelly are all colloids. Separating a colloid needs centrifugation, since filtration will not do it.

sections.h: The Tyndall effect — the test that tells them apart
paras: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of a beam of light by particles in a mixture, which makes the path of the beam visible. It is the standard laboratory test in this chapter.

A true solution does NOT show the Tyndall effect — its particles are too small to scatter light, so the beam passes through invisibly. Colloids and suspensions both DO show it. This is why sunbeams are visible streaming through a dusty room or through fog, and why a torch beam is visible in milk but not in salt water.

sections.h: The full comparison
paras: Learn these five properties as a set; questions almost always ask for a table.
bullets: Nature — solution: homogeneous. Suspension: heterogeneous. Colloid: appears homogeneous but is heterogeneous.
Particle size — solution: less than 1 nm. Colloid: 1–1000 nm. Suspension: more than 100 nm and usually visible.
Stability — solution: stable, never settles. Colloid: stable, does not settle. Suspension: unstable, settles on standing.
Filtration — solution and colloid particles pass through filter paper. Suspension particles do not.
Tyndall effect — solution: absent. Colloid and suspension: present.

examples.t: Salt dissolved in water
examples.d: A solution. Transparent, stable, passes through filter paper and shows no Tyndall effect.

examples.t: Chalk powder stirred into water
examples.d: A suspension. The particles are visible, settle at the bottom and are caught by filter paper.

examples.t: Milk
examples.d: A colloid. It looks uniform but scatters light, and its fat droplets cannot be filtered out.

examples.t: A torch beam visible in fog but not in clear air
examples.d: The Tyndall effect. Fog is a colloid whose droplets scatter the light; the gases of clear air do not.

mistakes: Forgetting colloids as the third category. Almost every full-mark answer needs all three.
Saying a solution shows the Tyndall effect. It does not — that is precisely what distinguishes it from a colloid.
Claiming a colloid settles on standing. It does not; only a suspension does.
Thinking a colloid can be separated by ordinary filtration. It needs centrifugation.
Calling milk a solution because it looks uniform. Appearance is not the test — the Tyndall effect is.

quiz.q: Which of these does NOT show the Tyndall effect?
quiz.why: A true solution has particles smaller than 1 nm, too small to scatter light. Colloids and suspensions both scatter it.

quiz.q: Particles of a suspension:
quiz.why: Suspension particles are large and heavy enough to settle under gravity when left undisturbed — the mixture is unstable.

quiz.q: Milk is an example of a:
quiz.why: Milk's fat droplets are between 1 and 1000 nm, so it appears uniform, does not settle, but does scatter light.

quiz.q: A colloid can be separated by:
quiz.why: Colloidal particles pass through filter paper, so centrifugation is used to spin them out instead.

extraFaqs.q: What is the main difference between a solution and a suspension?
extraFaqs.a: A solution is a homogeneous mixture with particles smaller than 1 nm that never settle, pass through filter paper and do not scatter light. A suspension is heterogeneous, with particles larger than about 100 nm that settle on standing, are held back by filter paper and scatter light strongly.

extraFaqs.q: What is the Tyndall effect and why does it matter?
extraFaqs.a: It is the scattering of a beam of light by the particles of a mixture, which makes the beam's path visible. It matters because it is the simplest laboratory test to distinguish a true solution, which shows no Tyndall effect, from a colloid or suspension, which both do.

extraFaqs.q: Is a colloid homogeneous or heterogeneous?
extraFaqs.a: A colloid is heterogeneous in nature, even though it appears homogeneous to the naked eye. Its dispersed particles are distinct from the medium they are spread through, which is why it scatters light — but they are too small to be seen or to settle.

extraFaqs.q: Why does muddy water become clear on standing?
extraFaqs.a: Muddy water is a suspension. Its soil particles are large and dense enough that gravity pulls them to the bottom once the water is left undisturbed, leaving clearer water above. A solution would never separate this way.

applications.h: Why medicine bottles say "shake well before use"
applications.d: Many liquid medicines are suspensions: the active drug is not dissolved but dispersed as fine solid particles. Left standing, those particles settle to the bottom, so the first dose poured would be weak and the last dangerously strong. Shaking redistributes them evenly. A syrup that is a true solution — glucose in water, say — needs no such instruction, because dissolved particles never settle. The label tells you which type you are holding.

applications.h: How water is purified at a treatment plant
applications.d: Muddy river water is a suspension, and its large particles settle under gravity — the sedimentation step. Alum is added to make the finer colloidal particles clump into larger ones heavy enough to settle, a process called coagulation or flocculation. Filtration then removes what remains suspended. Note that no amount of filtering removes dissolved salts, because a true solution passes straight through filter paper; that needs distillation or reverse osmosis.

applications.h: The Tyndall effect in daily life
applications.d: Sunlight streaming through a gap in a forest canopy becomes visible because mist droplets scatter it. So do the beams of car headlights in fog, and a torch shone through milk. In each case a colloid is scattering the light. Shine the same torch through clear salt water and the beam is invisible, because a true solution’s particles are far too small to scatter. It is the simplest test that distinguishes the three mixture types.

applications.h: Why the sky is blue
applications.d: The atmosphere scatters shorter blue wavelengths more strongly than longer red ones, which is why the daytime sky is blue and why the sun looks red at sunrise and sunset, when its light travels through much more atmosphere and the blue has been scattered away. This is scattering by very fine particles and molecules — the same physical principle underlying the Tyndall effect you test in the laboratory.

boardQuestions.q: Distinguish between a true solution, a colloid and a suspension on the basis of particle size, appearance, stability, filterability and the Tyndall effect.
boardQuestions.a: A true solution has particles smaller than 1 nanometre. It is homogeneous and transparent, completely stable so the particles never settle, passes unchanged through filter paper, and does NOT show the Tyndall effect because its particles are too small to scatter light. A colloid has particles between 1 and 1000 nanometres. It appears homogeneous to the naked eye but is actually heterogeneous, is stable so it does not settle on standing, passes through ordinary filter paper but can be separated by centrifugation, and DOES show the Tyndall effect. A suspension has particles larger than about 100 nanometres, often visible to the naked eye. It is heterogeneous, unstable so the particles settle out on standing, is retained by filter paper, and also shows the Tyndall effect. Examples are salt water, milk and muddy water respectively.

boardQuestions.q: What is the Tyndall effect? Describe an experiment to demonstrate it.
boardQuestions.a: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of a beam of light by the particles of a colloid or suspension, which makes the path of the beam visible. To demonstrate it, take two beakers, one containing a true solution such as common salt in water and the other containing a colloid such as dilute milk or a starch solution. Place each in a dark room and shine a narrow beam of light from a torch through it, viewing at right angles to the beam. In the salt solution the beam is invisible, because the dissolved particles are smaller than 1 nanometre and cannot scatter light. In the milk the path of the beam is clearly visible as a bright track, because the colloidal particles are large enough to scatter it. The same effect is seen when sunlight enters a dusty room or passes through a forest canopy.

boardQuestions.q: Why must a suspension be shaken before use, but a solution need not be?
boardQuestions.a: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture whose particles are large and dense enough for gravity to pull them down, so on standing they settle at the bottom and the mixture becomes non-uniform. Shaking redistributes the particles so that each portion poured contains the intended amount. A true solution is homogeneous, with particles smaller than 1 nanometre that remain permanently dispersed among the solvent molecules and never settle, so its composition is identical throughout at all times and no shaking is required.

boardQuestions.q: Classify the following as solution, colloid or suspension: salt water, milk, muddy water, soda water, fog, chalk powder in water.
boardQuestions.a: Salt water is a true solution, because the sodium chloride dissolves completely into particles smaller than 1 nanometre. Milk is a colloid, an emulsion of liquid fat droplets dispersed in water, which is why it appears uniform but shows the Tyndall effect. Muddy water is a suspension, since the soil particles are large, visible and settle on standing. Soda water is a solution of carbon dioxide gas in water. Fog is a colloid, consisting of tiny liquid water droplets dispersed in air, an aerosol. Chalk powder in water is a suspension, because the chalk does not dissolve and settles out.

boardQuestions.q: How can the components of a suspension and of a colloid be separated?
boardQuestions.a: A suspension can be separated by ordinary filtration, because its particles are larger than the pores of filter paper and are therefore retained on it; simply allowing it to stand so the particles sediment will also partly separate it. A colloid cannot be separated by filtration, since its particles are small enough to pass through filter paper. It is separated by centrifugation, in which rapid spinning generates a force much larger than gravity and drives the dispersed particles to the bottom of the tube. Coagulation, for example by adding alum, can also make colloidal particles clump together until they are large enough to settle.

assertionReason.assertion: A true solution does not show the Tyndall effect.
assertionReason.reason: Its particles are smaller than 1 nm and cannot scatter light.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. Scattering requires particles comparable to the wavelength of light; solute particles are far too small.

assertionReason.assertion: Milk is a true solution because it looks uniform.
assertionReason.reason: A mixture that appears uniform to the eye is homogeneous.
assertionReason.why: The assertion is false — milk is a colloid, which is why it scatters light. The reason is also false as a general rule: appearance is not the test, since colloids look uniform while being heterogeneous.

assertionReason.assertion: Colloidal particles cannot be separated by filtration.
assertionReason.reason: Colloidal particles are smaller than the pores of filter paper.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and correctly linked. This is why centrifugation, not filtration, is used to separate a colloid.

assertionReason.assertion: Muddy water becomes clear on standing.
assertionReason.reason: Suspensions are unstable and their particles settle under gravity.
assertionReason.why: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion. This sedimentation is the first step in water treatment.

glossary.def: A homogeneous mixture with particles smaller than 1 nm. Stable, transparent, no Tyndall effect.
A heterogeneous mixture with particles 1-1000 nm that LOOKS homogeneous. Stable, shows the Tyndall effect.
A heterogeneous mixture with particles above ~100 nm. Unstable, settles on standing, retained by filter paper.
The scattering of a light beam by colloid or suspension particles, making the beam path visible.
Uniform in composition throughout, with no visible boundary between components.
Not uniform — the components remain physically distinct.
The substance spread through a colloid, e.g. fat droplets in milk.
The substance a colloid is dispersed in, e.g. water in milk.
A colloid of one liquid dispersed in another, such as milk.
A colloid of solid or liquid particles dispersed in a gas, such as fog or smoke.
Rapid spinning used to separate a colloid, since filtration cannot.
Making colloidal particles clump together until heavy enough to settle, e.g. adding alum to water.

revision: THREE types, not two: SOLUTION (<1 nm), COLLOID (1-1000 nm), SUSPENSION (>100 nm).
Tyndall effect: solution NO, colloid YES, suspension YES. It is the quickest test.
Settles on standing: only the SUSPENSION. Solutions and colloids do not.
Filter paper stops only the SUSPENSION. Colloids need CENTRIFUGATION.
A colloid LOOKS homogeneous but IS heterogeneous. Appearance is not the test.
Milk, fog, smoke, ink, jelly = colloids. Muddy water, chalk in water = suspensions.
Salt water and soda water = true solutions. Filtration will never remove dissolved salt.
Alum coagulates colloidal particles so they clump and settle — the water-treatment step.

producer-vs-consumer.ncertRef: NCERT Class 10 Science, Chapter 15 — Our Environment.

explainers.term: Producers — the organisms that make their own food
paras: Producers, also called autotrophs, make their own food from simple inorganic substances. Green plants and algae do this by photosynthesis, using sunlight, carbon dioxide and water to build glucose and release oxygen. Some bacteria manage it chemically instead, without light.

Producers form the first trophic level of every food chain, and they are the only entry point for energy into an ecosystem. All the energy that every other organism uses was originally captured by a producer from sunlight — which is why removing producers would collapse the whole system.

explainers.term: Consumers — the organisms that depend on others
paras: Consumers, also called heterotrophs, cannot make their own food and must obtain it by eating other organisms. Every animal is a consumer, along with fungi and many bacteria.

Consumers are classified by what they eat. Herbivores such as deer, goats and grasshoppers eat plants directly and are primary consumers. Carnivores such as frogs and snakes eat other animals and are secondary or tertiary consumers depending on their position. Omnivores such as humans and bears eat both, and parasites live on or in a host, feeding off it.

sections.h: Decomposers — the group students forget
paras: Decomposers are bacteria and fungi that break down the dead remains of plants and animals into simple inorganic substances, returning nutrients to the soil where producers can use them again.

They are what makes the ecosystem cyclic. Without decomposers, nutrients would stay locked inside dead bodies, the soil would be exhausted and producers could not grow. Many students list only producers and consumers and lose the mark for decomposers.

sections.h: Food chains, food webs and trophic levels
paras: A food chain is a single sequence of who eats whom: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle. Each step in it is a trophic level, with producers always at the first.

In reality organisms eat several different things, so many food chains interconnect to form a food web. A food web is more realistic and more stable than a single chain, because if one species disappears others can still be eaten instead.

sections.h: The ten per cent law, and why chains are short
paras: Only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next. The other 90% is lost, mostly as heat during respiration, and in movement, digestion and undigested material.

This is why food chains rarely have more than four or five links: after four steps so little of the original energy remains that it cannot support another level. It also explains why the number of organisms usually falls sharply at each higher level.

Energy flow through an ecosystem is unidirectional — it enters from the Sun, passes up the trophic levels and is lost as heat. It never cycles back, unlike nutrients, which decomposers do return. A related idea is biomagnification: harmful chemicals such as pesticides are not broken down, so they become more concentrated at each successive trophic level, and top consumers accumulate the most.

examples.t: Grass in a field
examples.d: A producer. It builds its own food by photosynthesis and occupies the first trophic level.

examples.t: A grasshopper eating that grass
examples.d: A primary consumer, and a herbivore — the second trophic level.

examples.t: A snake eating a frog that ate the grasshopper
examples.d: A tertiary consumer. Very little of the grass's original energy remains by this point.

examples.t: Fungi growing on a fallen log
examples.d: Decomposers, returning the log's locked-up nutrients to the soil for producers to reuse.

mistakes: Listing only producers and consumers and omitting decomposers.
Calling all plants producers without exception. A few, such as the pitcher plant supplementing its nitrogen, and fully parasitic plants like Cuscuta, do not fit neatly.
Saying energy cycles through an ecosystem. Energy flow is unidirectional; it is nutrients that cycle.
Applying the ten per cent law backwards. Ten per cent passes on; ninety per cent is lost.
Assuming a food web is just a longer food chain. A web is many interconnected chains, which is what makes it more stable.

extraFaqs.q: What is the difference between a producer and a consumer?
extraFaqs.a: Producers are autotrophs that make their own food from simple inorganic substances, usually by photosynthesis, and occupy the first trophic level. Consumers are heterotrophs that cannot make their own food and must eat other organisms to obtain it. All the energy consumers use was originally captured by producers.

extraFaqs.q: Are decomposers producers or consumers?
extraFaqs.a: Neither. Decomposers form a separate group. Bacteria and fungi break down dead plant and animal remains into simple substances that return to the soil, allowing producers to use them again. They are what makes nutrient flow cyclic rather than one-way.

extraFaqs.q: What is the ten per cent law?
extraFaqs.a: It states that only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next, with roughly 90% lost mainly as heat during respiration and in movement and digestion. It is the reason food chains rarely exceed four or five levels.

extraFaqs.q: What is biomagnification?
extraFaqs.a: It is the increasing concentration of harmful, non-biodegradable substances such as pesticides at each successive trophic level. Because these chemicals are not broken down or excreted, they accumulate in the bodies of organisms, so top consumers — including humans — end up carrying the highest concentrations.
